messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 48
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Roofer
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 47

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Media / News: Related news, Auditory/Mechanical: Motorcycle noise, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress, Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control, Busyness: I work hard at keeping busy with other things
  Memory: More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Manaia was 48 years old, a roofer by trade, and he had spent the last three decades of his life on the sun-baked rooftops of suburban Phoenix. He was a big man, broad-shouldered and quiet, and he had been married to his wife, Leilani, for twenty-two years. The assault happened four years ago, after a company barbecue at a colleague’s house. He had drunk too much, and a younger man on the crew had offered to drive him home. Instead, the man pulled into an empty lot behind a strip mall and raped him in the cab of the truck. Manaia had not told anyone. He had walked home, showered, and told Leilani he had fallen off a ladder. The shame was immediate and absolute. He had come to believe that what happened had made him less of a man, and that if anyone knew—especially his wife—she would see him as weak, as broken, as someone who had let it happen.

In the weeks that followed, the world began to narrow. The first thing he noticed was the alcohol smell. A single whiff of beer on a client’s breath would send his stomach into a cold knot, and he would find himself standing rigid on the edge of a roof, his hands shaking around a nail gun. Then came the motorcycle noise. A Harley rumbling past at a traffic light would hit him like a punch—the low, vibrating growl was the same sound that had filled the truck cab just before the man’s hand had clamped over his mouth. Manaia began to flinch at the television, too. A news report about a sexual assault trial, even one involving a stranger and a woman, would flood him with a heat so intense he had to leave the room. These triggers did not just disturb him; they pulled the memory forward. Sometimes, when the motorcycle passed, the whole scene would snap into his mind with a clarity that felt more real than the roof he was standing on—the smell of the vinyl seat, the pressure of the man’s knee against his thigh, the exact pitch of the man’s laugh. At other times, the emotional intensity would arrive without any image at all: a wave of grief so sudden and total that he would have to sit down, his eyes burning, unable to explain to his foreman why he had stopped working.

To manage this, Manaia developed a set of habits that he told himself were just discipline. He started restricting his eating, controlling every meal with precision—the same three foods at the same times every day—because the structure gave him a feeling of order in a world that felt unmoored. He also began to avoid any physical stress that mimicked the sensations of the assault: he stopped lifting weights at the gym, he refused to run, and on the job he would hand off the heaviest bundles of shingles to younger men, claiming his back was sore. The thing that consumed most of his energy, however, was keeping busy. He would take on extra shifts, volunteer for the dirtiest jobs, and spend his evenings fixing things around the house until his hands ached. He told himself he was being productive, but the real reason was that stillness felt dangerous. When he stopped, the grief came. And when the grief came, he found himself scanning his environment for the next trigger—listening for the rumble of an engine, checking the breath of the man next to him at the hardware store, bracing himself for a news headline. The busier he stayed, the less often the memory surfaced. But the strategy had a cost. The constant vigilance exhausted him, and the grief, when it finally broke through, was worse each time, because he had been holding it at bay for so long. He had also begun to withdraw from Leilani. She wanted to go out for dinner, but the restaurant might have a bar, and the smell of alcohol was everywhere. He would say he was tired, and then lie awake for hours, listening to the house settle, waiting for the next wave to hit.

What finally brought Manaia to a therapist’s office was a morning in late July. He had been on a roof, the sun already brutal at eight a.m., and a delivery truck had backfired in the street below. The sound had sent him into a full flashback—he had dropped to his knees on the hot tar paper, his breath gone, his hands pressed flat against the shingles. His foreman had called his name three times before Manaia heard him. That night, for the first time, he told Leilani a partial truth: that something bad had happened to him years ago, and that he could not stop thinking about it. She held his hand and said nothing, and the grief he felt in that moment was so enormous that he finally understood he could not outrun it. He was afraid of what the therapy would require—of saying the words out loud, of being seen as a victim—but he was more afraid of the roof, of the truck, of the sound of an engine that was waiting for him every day.
